homology.name: Biceps brachii
homology.human: Biceps — but theirs cannot turn the palm up, because their forearm bones barely rotate.
homology.dog: A straightforward working elbow flexor, with a normal fleshy belly along the front of the arm.
homology.cat: Retains real rotation — a cat can turn its paw to grip and to wash its face, which a horse can never do.
homology.horse: Mostly TENDON rather than muscle, and part of the stay apparatus: a fibrous band runs straight through it so the shoulder and elbow can be locked open without muscular work.

homology.name: Biceps femoris
homology.human: Biceps femoris — the outer hamstring.
homology.dog: The obvious outline of a dog's upper hind leg.
homology.cat: Long and elastic; part of the cat's spring.
homology.horse: Huge, and reaches much further forward onto the sacrum than a human hamstring does. The shape of a horse's thigh from behind is this muscle and semitendinosus side by side.

homology.name: Brachialis
homology.human: Brachialis — same muscle, spiralling round the arm bone the same way.
homology.dog: Distinct band lateral to the biceps.
homology.cat: Well developed; a cat pulls with its forelimbs constantly.
homology.horse: Present but modest — flexing the elbow is not a big part of what a horse leg does.

homology.name: Brachiocephalicus
homology.human: Roughly your sternocleidomastoid plus the front edge of your trapezius, fused into one strap because the collarbone that would separate them is missing or tiny.
homology.dog: One continuous strap with only a faint tendinous line where a collarbone would be. It is the muscle you are feeling either side of a dog's neck.
homology.cat: Split more clearly by the cat's small real collarbone, giving the shoulder more independent reach and rotation than a dog gets.
homology.horse: No collarbone at all, so this is one long uninterrupted band from poll to arm. Its lower border is the visible groove on a horse's neck where the jugular runs — the landmark you use to raise the vein.

homology.name: Cutaneous trunci
homology.human: No real human equivalent. The nearest leftovers in you are the small muscle under the skin of the palm and the sheet in your neck — you cannot twitch your back skin, and they can.
homology.dog: Well developed over the trunk. The "panniculus" skin-twitch reflex is a standard part of a neurological exam.
homology.cat: Present and brisk; also part of the classic rippling-skin response.
homology.horse: Very well developed — this is the muscle doing the fly-shudder along a horse's side, and its reflex maps the nerve supply of the trunk neatly.

homology.name: Deltoid
homology.human: Deltoid — but yours wraps the whole shoulder because it also grips your collarbone.
homology.dog: A clear two-part muscle over the point of the shoulder.
homology.cat: Relatively large, and with the clavicle it gives the cat genuine sideways reach — a cat can bat sideways, a horse cannot.
homology.horse: Comparatively small. A horse's forelimb swings almost purely forwards and backwards, so a muscle for sideways movement has little to do.

homology.name: Extensor carpi radialis
homology.human: Extensor carpi radialis — the muscle on the thumb side of your forearm that cocks your wrist back.
homology.dog: Fleshy well down the forearm, and easy to feel tightening when the paw is lifted.
homology.cat: Fleshy and mobile, matching the cat's flexible wrist.
homology.horse: Becomes tendon high up and runs as a cord straight down the front of the cannon — one of the cords you can feel and follow on a standing horse.

homology.name: Common digital extensor
homology.human: Extensor digitorum — the tendons you can see fanning across the back of your hand.
homology.dog: Fans into four tendons, one per weight-bearing toe.
homology.cat: Four tendons, and the cat can spread its toes and put out its claws independently.
homology.horse: ONE tendon to ONE toe. Everything that used to serve four digits now serves a single hoof — which is why a single extensor injury in a horse is a whole-limb problem.

homology.name: Fibularis (peroneus) longus
homology.human: Fibularis (peroneus) longus — the muscle running down the outside of your calf behind the ankle bone.
homology.dog: Present and functional, running with a complete fibula.
homology.cat: Present and well developed — part of how a cat turns its hind foot to grip and to climb down head-first.
homology.horse: NOT PRESENT as a working muscle. The horse has reduced its second shin bone to a splint fused to the tibia, and the muscles that used to turn the foot went with it — a horse cannot rotate its foot at all.

homology.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
homology.human: Flexor carpi ulnaris — the little-finger-side wrist flexor.
homology.dog: Easy to palpate on the caudal forearm.
homology.cat: Prominent; a cat flexes its wrist through a wide range.
homology.horse: Short-bellied with a long tendon, in keeping with the horse's pattern of putting muscle high and cord low.

homology.name: Deep digital flexor
homology.human: Flexor digitorum profundus — the deep tendon that bends the end joint of your fingers.
homology.dog: Fleshy for much of its length; flexes the toes for grip and digging.
homology.cat: Works with the claw mechanism — the same pull that flexes the toe protrudes the claw.
homology.horse: The cord down the back of the cannon, held in check by a ligament so it can support the fetlock without muscular effort. This tendon and its check ligament are among the most commonly injured structures in a performance horse.

homology.name: Superficial digital flexor
homology.human: Flexor digitorum superficialis — the tendon that bends the middle joint of your fingers and toes.
homology.dog: Has a real muscle belly and works as a muscle.
homology.cat: Fleshy and mobile, and it works with the claw mechanism when the cat grips with a hind foot.
homology.horse: Almost entirely TENDINOUS in the hind limb, and it is the second half of the reciprocal apparatus with gastrocnemius. In the FRONT limb its counterpart is the most commonly strained tendon in racing and jumping.

homology.name: Gastrocnemius
homology.human: Gastrocnemius — your calf muscle, ending in your Achilles tendon.
homology.dog: Fleshy calf; a ruptured Achilles here drops the hock to the ground, which is unmistakable.
homology.cat: Powerful and quick — the main muscle behind a cat's vertical leap.
homology.horse: Muscular high up and tendon almost all the way down, and it is a working part of the RECIPROCAL apparatus: hock and stifle in a horse are mechanically chained, so one cannot bend without the other. That chain is what lets a horse rest a hind leg while standing.

homology.name: Gluteus medius
homology.human: Gluteus medius — but in you it mostly steadies the pelvis when you stand on one leg, and in them it is a propulsion engine.
homology.dog: Large; a sprinting dog is largely this muscle and the hamstrings.
homology.cat: Fast and powerful for its size — the launch of a vertical jump.
homology.horse: Enormous, and it runs FORWARD over the loin well past the pelvis, which no human gluteal does. This forward extension is why a horse's croup is muscled all the way to the back of the saddle.

homology.name: Superficial gluteal
homology.human: Gluteus maximus — your biggest buttock muscle, which is far larger in you than in any of them because you stand upright.
homology.dog: Small and superficial over the point of the hip.
homology.cat: Small — the cat's power sits deeper.
homology.horse: Fused with a strip running down to the thigh, forming one continuous band. The rounded outline of a horse's rump is this muscle over gluteus medius.

homology.name: Gracilis
homology.human: Gracilis — the inner-thigh strap that pulls your legs together.
homology.dog: Covers most of the inner thigh; the first sheet you meet approaching the femoral vessels.
homology.cat: Broad and thin, sheeting most of the inner thigh under very loose skin.
homology.horse: Wide; the inside of a horse's thigh is largely gracilis over semimembranosus.

homology.name: Iliocostalis
homology.human: Iliocostalis — the outer column of your erector spinae.
homology.dog: Contributes to the sideways whip of a turning dog.
homology.cat: Very active in the cat's side-to-side twist mid-leap.
homology.horse: Present but overshadowed by longissimus; a horse deliberately limits sideways bend through the trunk.

homology.name: Infraspinatus
homology.human: Infraspinatus — the rotator-cuff muscle behind your shoulder blade's ridge.
homology.dog: Palpable behind the shoulder ridge; a common site of shoulder lameness.
homology.cat: Fine and very mobile — the cat trades bracing strength here for a shoulder that can rotate and reach.
homology.horse: Very strong; acts as the lateral collateral ligament of the shoulder, which is why an infraspinatus problem reads as instability rather than simple soreness.

homology.name: Latissimus dorsi
homology.human: Latissimus dorsi — the same broad back muscle, doing the same pull-the-arm-backwards job.
homology.dog: Powerful — this is a lot of the drive in a dog dragging itself up over an obstacle.
homology.cat: Very strong for the animal's size; a cat climbing uses it hard.
homology.horse: Broad and flat, and it lies under the back of the saddle. Its rear border is the usual site for an intramuscular injection high on the neck's counterpart at the rear.

homology.name: Longissimus dorsi
homology.human: Erector spinae — the long columns either side of your backbone.
homology.dog: Works with a fairly flexible back — a galloping dog flexes and extends its spine with every stride.
homology.cat: Extremely elastic. The cat's bound is largely this muscle and the loin unrolling.
homology.horse: The horse's back is built to stay STIFF, and this is the muscle that keeps it that way. It sits directly under the saddle, so back pain in a ridden horse is a longissimus question until proven otherwise.

homology.name: Masseter
homology.human: Masseter — the same muscle you can feel bulge when you clench.
homology.dog: Powerful but short-levered: a dog is built to grip and tear, so the jaw shuts fast rather than grinding.
homology.cat: Proportionally the largest of the three. A cat's whole skull is short, which turns the masseter into a very short, very strong lever for a killing bite.
homology.horse: Enormous and deep, and it works sideways as much as up and down — a horse grinds fibre for hours, so this is a chewing motor rather than a biting one. A swollen masseter is a classic thing to check on a horse's cheek.

homology.name: External abdominal oblique
homology.human: External oblique — the same sheet down your flank.
homology.dog: Covers most of the visible flank.
homology.cat: Thin but very extensible — a cat can fold almost double.
homology.horse: Broad, and its lower edge and the "flank fold" are standard landmarks. Colic pain shows up as guarding here.

homology.name: Omotransversarius
homology.human: Closest match is levator scapulae — but yours cannot pull the shoulder blade forward the way this one does, because your collarbone anchors it.
homology.dog: Clear flat band along the lower neck, easy to find under the skin.
homology.cat: Prominent — part of how a stalking cat slides its shoulder blade so far forward.
homology.horse: Blends with the brachiocephalicus and is harder to separate as a distinct muscle on the standing animal.

homology.name: Deep pectoral
homology.human: The lower, sternal part of your pectoralis major.
homology.dog: Substantial; contributes to the sling along with serratus.
homology.cat: Assists the cat in pulling itself up onto a ledge.
homology.horse: Large. Its lower edge is a landmark for the girth line, and girth galls sit exactly over it.

homology.name: Superficial pectoral
homology.human: The upper part of your pectoralis major.
homology.dog: Gives a broad-chested dog its front. Divided into two clear bellies.
homology.cat: Slim, matching the cat's narrow chest.
homology.horse: Builds the muscular V you see between a horse's front legs from in front.

homology.name: Quadriceps femoris
homology.human: Quadriceps — same four heads, same kneecap tendon.
homology.dog: Big; drives the extension phase of the stride.
homology.cat: Explosive rather than enduring.
homology.horse: Very large, and part of the stay apparatus: it can hitch the kneecap over a ridge on the thigh bone so the hind limb locks straight and the horse can sleep standing. A stifle that will not unlock is a real clinical presentation.

homology.name: Rectus abdominis
homology.human: Rectus abdominis — your "six-pack" strap, with the same cross-bands.
homology.dog: Strong; part of the deep tuck-up behind the ribs.
homology.cat: Very strong relative to size — a cat pulling its hind legs up under itself mid-jump is using this hard.
homology.horse: Long and important for foaling and for supporting a very heavy gut. A dropped, pendulous belly in an older horse is this muscle and its sheath giving way.

homology.name: Rhomboideus
homology.human: Rhomboids, plus a neck portion you do not have.
homology.dog: Well developed; helps hold the trunk up between the shoulder blades.
homology.cat: Long neck portion — it can hoist the shoulder blade above the line of the back, which is exactly what you see in a cat creeping forward.
homology.horse: Thick and short, working with serratus ventralis to keep a half-tonne trunk hanging between the blades.

homology.name: Sartorius
homology.human: Sartorius — the long strap that runs diagonally across the front of your thigh.
homology.dog: Two clear parts on the front of the thigh.
homology.cat: Broad and flat, covering much of the inner thigh.
homology.horse: Thin, and it helps roof the passage where the big vessels enter the hind limb — a landmark rather than a mover.

homology.name: Semimembranosus
homology.human: Semimembranosus — the deep inner hamstring.
homology.dog: Forms much of the inner thigh, and is the mass you push aside to reach the femoral vessels.
homology.cat: Slim and deep, tucked behind the other hamstrings on the inside of the thigh.
homology.horse: Thick; part of the mass you feel on the inside of a horse's thigh.

homology.name: Semitendinosus
homology.human: Semitendinosus — the inner hamstring, with the same long tendon.
homology.dog: Defines the back edge of the thigh.
homology.cat: Long-bellied, strongly flexes the knee for the tuck of a jump.
homology.horse: Its back border is the visible edge of the hindquarter seen from the side, and the gap between it and biceps femoris is a standard injection site.

homology.name: Serratus ventralis
homology.human: Serratus anterior — same muscle, completely different job, because you hang your arm off a collarbone and they do not.
homology.dog: Strong fan; takes the shock of every landing forelimb.
homology.cat: Elastic and mobile — it lets the trunk drop between the shoulder blades when a cat lands from a height.
homology.horse: The classic example of the thoracic sling, and one of the most important structures in the horse: it carries roughly sixty per cent of the animal's weight and is why a horse has no collarbone to shatter. Fatigue or damage here shows as a trunk that has sunk between the shoulder blades.

homology.name: Splenius
homology.human: Splenius capitis — the strap under the back of your neck.
homology.dog: Moderate. A dog carries its head roughly level, so this works mostly to steady rather than to hold up.
homology.cat: Light — a cat's head is small and its neck short.
homology.horse: Huge, and it works with the big elastic ligament of the neck (the nuchal ligament) which does much of the holding for free. That partnership is why a horse can carry a heavy head all day without tiring.

homology.name: Sternocephalicus
homology.human: The sternal half of your sternocleidomastoid.
homology.dog: Slim and paired, meeting its partner low on the throat.
homology.cat: Thin and easily missed; the cat leans on neck flexibility rather than pull here.
homology.horse: Forms the LOWER wall of the jugular groove, with the brachiocephalicus above it. Together they are the reason the vein is so easy to find on a horse.

homology.name: Supraspinatus
homology.human: Supraspinatus — the top rotator-cuff muscle.
homology.dog: Moderate; a stabiliser more than a mover.
homology.cat: Slim — the cat wants shoulder mobility, not rigidity.
homology.horse: Thick and, with infraspinatus, effectively replaces a shoulder joint capsule strong enough to hold half a tonne. In a horse this muscle IS the shoulder ligament.

homology.name: Temporalis
homology.human: Temporalis — the muscle at your temple that moves when you chew.
homology.dog: Big enough to build a ridge along the top of the skull in strong-jawed breeds — that crest is there purely to give this muscle more room.
homology.cat: Very large for the head size, and the main reason a cat's skull looks domed between the ears.
homology.horse: Comparatively modest. A grazer needs endurance and sideways grinding more than a crushing vertical bite, so the masseter dominates instead.

homology.name: Tensor fasciae latae
homology.human: Tensor fasciae latae — the same small muscle at the front of your hip, tightening the same band down the outside of the thigh.
homology.dog: Forms the front edge of the flank triangle.
homology.cat: Slim — a cat swings its hind limb forward with the hip and spine rather than with this small muscle.
homology.horse: Prominent, and its front border is a clear landmark on the standing horse — the visible fold in front of the thigh.

homology.name: Teres major
homology.human: Teres major — same muscle, same partnership with latissimus.
homology.dog: Clear strap on the inner shoulder.
homology.cat: Strong; part of the pull a climbing cat generates.
homology.horse: Present and functional but hidden deep against the chest wall.

homology.name: Cranial tibial
homology.human: Tibialis anterior — the muscle on the front of your shin that lifts your foot.
homology.dog: Fleshy along most of the shin, and the muscle a dog uses to pick its paw up over an obstacle.
homology.cat: Well developed; the cat picks its feet up precisely.
homology.horse: Its tendon splits and one branch, the peroneus tertius, is a pure fibrous cord that mechanically ties hock to stifle. A torn cord shows up as the hock extending while the stifle stays bent — impossible in a sound horse.

homology.name: Trapezius
homology.human: Trapezius — but yours reaches your collarbone, and theirs stops at the shoulder blade.
homology.dog: Thin and broad; you are feeling it whenever you scratch a dog over the shoulder.
homology.cat: Divided into distinct parts around the clavicle, which is part of the cat's extra shoulder freedom.
homology.horse: Thin over a very large area, and it lies exactly where a saddle sits — so soreness here is a saddle-fit question before it is anything else.

homology.name: Triceps brachii
homology.human: Triceps — same three heads, same job.
homology.dog: Bulky and obvious; the biggest muscle of the canine forelimb.
homology.cat: Strong and fast — this is the push in a cat's pounce.
homology.horse: Massive. It works with the shoulder muscles as part of the standing mechanism that lets a horse doze on its feet with almost no muscular effort.

species.name: Dog
species.notes: Deep-chested, digitigrade, built for endurance trotting. The shoulder blade swings freely against the ribcage — dogs have no working collarbone.

species.name: Cat
species.notes: Small, light and extremely mobile through the shoulder and spine. A cat keeps a small floating collarbone, and its scapula slides high on the ribcage when it stalks.

species.name: Horse
species.stance: Unguligrade — stands on one hoofed toe per limb
species.notes: Unguligrade — it stands on the tip of one finger and one toe per limb. Long cannon bones, a huge hindquarter, and a trunk slung between the shoulder blades by muscle alone.
